items.title: When Neutrality Becomes Silence: McGill’s Responsibility to Protect Political Dissent
items.author: Lisa Banti
items.excerpt: McGill University encourages its students to think critically, question authority, and engage with the political issues that shape the world around them. Its own teaching guidelines emphasize questioning assumptions and examining competing perspectives, while its Statement of
items.leadExcerpt: McGill University encourages its students to think critically, question authority, and engage with the political issues that shape the world around them. Its own teaching guidelines emphasize questioning assumptions and examining competing perspectives, while its Statement of Academic Freedom recognizes the right to criticize university policies and administration. However, when students turn that same critical attention toward McGill’s own decisions, the university’s commitment to open debate becomes more complicated.

items.leadExcerpt: Any artist’s willingness to share the custody of their music must not be taken as a sign of it being impersonal. “It’s not mine, it’s ours,” Kline tells Radio TinTin, reflecting on releasing her music to the public. Kline has made a career out of confessional songwriting, creating lyrical and musical projects that are diary-like in tone — a diary that was never meant to reach millions of people. Reaching millions of people is exactly what happened, however, when her 2016 song “Fool” went viral on TikTok in early 2021. It has now appeared in 367 thousand total videos on the platform, and counts over 220 million streams on Spotify.

items.title: “It’s Our Livelihood”: AMUSE Pushes for Job Security at McGill
items.author: Lorin Kamaci
items.excerpt: The Association of McGill University Support Employees (AMUSE) is pushing for more consistent rules on discipline, scheduling, and paid hours, saying casual employees face varying practices across McGill departments. These concerns form part of its ongoing negotiations with the
items.leadExcerpt: Courtesy of AMUSE The Association of McGill University Support Employees (AMUSE) is pushing for more consistent rules on discipline, scheduling, and paid hours, saying casual employees face varying practices across McGill departments. These concerns form part of its ongoing negotiations with the university, which most recently met with the union on October 5 to discuss disciplinary procedures, probation, and hiring practices, with several issues remaining unresolved. According to its bargaining team, AMUSE represents approximately 1,300 to 1,600 casual employees, employees hired on a temporary or occasional basis, at McGill. Its collective agreement expired on May 31, 2025. The union developed its bargaining strategy through member surveys conducted in 2024 and 2025, as well as a special general meeting in September 2025.

items.leadExcerpt: L’Entracte is both a successor in this lineage of student-run venues, and a registered nonprofit. “All of the [proceeds are] distributed to musicians, to artists, to making a better venue,” said Dumouchel. While employees have standard wages, the leadership team works on a volunteer basis. “Since this is a nonprofit, community is everything,” Dumouchel added. The Daily spoke with Kevin Dean, a longtime McGill professor and staple within the Montreal jazz scene. “[L’Entracte] is a very ambitious project, butit has great potential and they seem to be on the right track.” Dean, who has lent his Hammond B3 organ and piano to the venue, says he’s keen to help out where he can. “It would be nice to have three full-time jazz clubs in town.” A virtuosic trumpet player and band leader in his own right, Dean runs a Sunday organ night at the venue twice a month, and regularly collaborates with student musicians.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Journalism: The Daily’s Stance
items.author: The editorial team
items.excerpt: In October 1995, M.J. Milloy — then-Coordinating Editor of The McGill Daily — reached out to former editors asking for a statement on what the Daily meant to them. Joan Mandell (BA 1979), co- founder of Al Fajr, the first Palestinian-produced English-language newspaper in the
items.leadExcerpt: The Daily has often described itself as just that: an opportunity that enables students to partake in the processes of independent reporting and collaborative editing. Part of the Daily’s mission has always been to encourage students to develop a critical journalistic eye. Today, the art of refining those “philosophical, political, aesthetic, literary and social values” has been interrupted by the Artificial Intelligence (AI) models that have infiltrated our academic spaces. AI has significantly shaped the way McGill students across various faculties approach learning; whether in drafting, editing, researching, or coding. Hence, McGill, which only has loose guidelines for professors and no enforeceable university-wide policy, faces an epidemic of unconstrained AI usage.

items.title: The Rocky Horror Picture Show Comes to McGill
items.author: Sonia Berman
items.excerpt: As the Halloween spirit crept in and neighborhood foliage shifted to an auburn hue, you may have seen crimson posters advertising Rocky Horror McGill on your walk to campus through Milton Parc or, perhaps, in the lavatory at McLennan Library.
items.leadExcerpt: While a midnight showing on Halloween is the classic experience, Rocky Horror productions are a year-round event. This year, for the first time, a collection of students, rather than any specific interest group or club, organized and hosted its very own live showing. On Friday, October 30 2026, I donned my costume (Magenta) and headed to the Rocky Horror live-showing in Leacock 132. Doors opened at 7:00 PM. Last-minute tickets were sold at the door, as well as individual prop bags. “The props that we [use] will definitely cause laughs,” said Potamia.

items.author: Enid Kohler
items.excerpt: Good People is a bi-weekly article series highlighting McGill students doing community-oriented work on and around campus. Because it’ s important to celebrate good people doing good things.
items.leadExcerpt: Image courtesy of Aidan Licoppe (centre) Aidan Licoppe Gen-Z created app R3ACH aims to combat loneliness and foster friendshipsamong young people Good People is a bi-weekly article series highlighting McGill students doing community-oriented work on and around campus. Because it’ s important to celebrate good people doing good things. Why is it so hard to reach out? It is a simple question but one that resonated deeply with Aidan Licoppe, the co- founder and head of technology of the R3ACH app. With a background in coding and machine learning, Licoppe started to think about in-person social connection more seriously during the second year of his master’s program in experimental medicine at McGill. Licoppe realized it was becoming more difficult for young people to form new friendships as screen time and social media increasingly eclipse face-to-face hangouts.

items.sourceImageCredit: Photo : Image Courtesy of Kate Hansen
items.leadExcerpt: It has been nearly a month since the Prize’s announcement, when I find myself conducting an interview of my own, and the irony of discussing his media attention is not lost on me. Journalists, myself included, seem keen to contextualize Carson’s win as a national achievement: she is only the nineteenth-ever Canadian Nobel Laureate, and only the second-ever in the category of literature. More important to me than Carson’s citizenship, however, is the Montreal of it all; interviewing MacLaren in McGill’s McCall MacBain Arts Building, I am thinking of all the times she may have walked these halls herself, in her time as a faculty member of the Department of Classics.

items.excerpt: Quoi de mieux pour profiter de l’Halloween qu’un bon film d’horreur ? Et québécois, qui plus est ? Pour l’occasion, Quartier Libre retourne dans le temps et propose un film québécois de 1996 avec des vampires, Karmina !
items.leadExcerpt: Quoi de mieux pour profiter de l’Halloween qu’un bon film d’horreur ? Et québécois, qui plus est ? Pour l’occasion, Quartier Libre retourne dans le temps et propose un film québécois de 1996 avec des vampires ! Principalement tournée à Montréal, l’histoire de Karmina débute en Transylvanie, dans un château où des dizaines de vampires sont réunis pour célébrer le mariage de la protagoniste. Karmina (Isabelle Cyr), alors promise à Vlad (Yves Pelletier), un vampire communiste, décide de fuguer plutôt que de se rendre à l’autel. Elle voyage jusqu’à Montréal, emportant avec elle son lit-cercueil, qui atterrit sur le carrousel des bagages à l’aéroport Montréal-Trudeau, devant les douaniers incrédules. L’un d’eux, Ghislain (Gildor Roy), inspecte le passeport de Karmina et lui donne la permission d’entrer au pays, non sans avoir été ensorcelé par cette dernière.
